paragraphs.source_en: Teti may have been followed by King Userkara (2323-2321 BC), although his existence can be disputed. Some confusion may be due to the fact that Pepy I (Horus Merytawy, 2321-2287 BC), the son of Teti and Queen Iput, was called Nefersahor in the first part of his reign. This was his 'prenomen' or 'throne name', received at his coronation, preceded by the title nesu-bit ('he of the sedge and bee') and enclosed in an oval cartouche. Later he changed it to Meryra. The 'nomen' or 'birth name', Pepy (the number that conventionally follows is ours, and was never used by the ancient Egyptians), predated his accession to the throne; it was introduced by the title sa Ra ('son of the god Ra') and was also written in a cartouche. Egypt's internal situation now began to change. The king's position remained theoretically unaffected, but there can be no doubt that difficulties appeared.

The king's person was no longer untouchable: a biographical text of Weni, a high THE OLD K I N G D O M 105 court official, mentions an unsuccessful plot against Pepy I inspired by one of his queens late in his reign. Her name is not given, but marriage politics were known: in his declining years, the king married two sisters, both called Ankhnes-meryra ('King Meryra [Pepy I] lives for her'). Their father Khui was an influential official at Abydos.

paragraphs.source_en: These were dramatic events, but the growth of power and influence of local administrators (especially in Upper Egypt, further away from the capital) and the corresponding weakening of the royal authority may have had less dramatic, but potentially much more serious, consequences. A new office of'overseer of Upper Egypt' was created late in the 5th Dynasty.
